newsitem.title: EU: EFTA court sets limits on employers' duty to pay premiums.
newsitem.headline: EFTA court sets limits on employers' duty to pay premiums.

text.p: INFORMATION NOTE PREPARED BY EFTA COURT
EFTA Court gives two rulings on important issues of European labour law

On 25 September, 1996, the EFTA Court rendered two advisory opinions on the Interpretation of Council Directive 77/287/EEC of 14 February, 1977, on the approximation of the laws of the Member States relating to the safeguarding of employees' rights in the event of transfers of undertakings, businesses or parts of businesses. The Court held that (1) depending on the circumstances the replacement of a service provider may constitute a transfer in the sense of the directive and (2) an obligation of the transferor to pay premiums to a supplementary pension scheme concerning old-age, invalidity and survivor's benefits it not transferred.
The Gulating Court of Appeals and the City Court of Stavanger in Norway had requested advisory opinions in cases pending before them.

The case before the Gulating Court of Appeals concerns a claim by Mr Eilert Eidesund that his present employer, Stavanger Catering A/S, should pay certain pension insurance premiums, which his former employer had paid into an insurance scheme, apparently on the basis of a local collective agreement with the employer. A similar action was brought by Mr Torgeir Langeland against Norske Fabricom A/S. Mr Eidesund had been employed by a company providing catering and cleaning services, Mr Langeland by a company providing plumbing services, on oil-drilling platforms in the North Sea. In the case Eidesund, after termination of the service contract a new company, Stavanger Catering A/S, obtained a contract to provide the same services. In the case Langeland, the undertaking was purchased by a new service provider, Norske Fabricom A/S.

The Court of Justice of the European Communities has been occupied with the concept of transfer in Article 1 of the directive in numerous cases. But none of these cases deal directly with the situation where an alleged transfer consists of a succession of two independent service providers. The EFTA Court noted that the supply of services or goods to one among several customers would normally not qualify as a distinct part of the supplier's business within the meaning of the directive. The same holds true of the loss of one customer to a competing company.

The EFTA Court held that Article 1 (1) of the Directive is to be interpreted so as to mean that, where catering services for an undertaking have by contract been entrusted to a company, the termination of that contract and the conclusion of a new contract for the same services with another company does not exclude the directive from being applicable. In order to determine that there is a transfer of undertaking in the meaning of the directive, an economic entity with its own identity must be transferred and this identity must be retained. In order to ascertain whether these conditions are fulfilled in a case such as the one at hand, it is necessary to determine whether or not tangible assets, such as buildings and moveable property, or intangible assets, such as patents or know-how, are transferred, the value and the nature of the assets, whether or not a majority of the employees, or employees with a special expertise or experience, are taken over, whether customers are transferred, the degree of similarity between the activities carried an before and after the transfer, and the period, if any, for which the activities were suspended.

The EFTA Court further ruled that according to Article 3 (3) of the directive, the employer's obligation to pay premiums to supplementary pension schemes for an employee is not transferred to the new employer. The accrual of pension benefits and the payment of pension premiums are inseparable. It would be without any economic sense to require premium payments to be made when no further benefits are to accrue. From this must follow that the transferor's obligation to pay premiums towards old-age, invalidity and survivors' benefits, is excluded from the transfer.

Further information is available from Meinhard Novak, Legal Secretary at the EFTA Court (Phone 352 42108 323 - Fax 352 434389). It should be noted that no comment on the cases can be made by the Court.
